question_text: What kind of object is the Sun?
choices: A star
A planet
A comet
A moon
correct_answer: A star
explanation: The Sun is the star at the center of our solar system. It makes light and heat through nuclear fusion.
traps: Thinking the Sun is a planet because it appears to move across our sky.

question_text: What does a planet do when it rotates?
choices: It spins around an axis
It travels once around a moon
It changes into a star
It moves from one galaxy to another
correct_answer: It spins around an axis
explanation: Rotation is the spinning of an object around an imaginary line called its axis.
traps: Confusing a planet's spin with its orbit around the Sun.

question_text: What does it mean when Earth completes one revolution around the Sun?
choices: Earth has completed one orbit
Earth has spun once on its axis
The Moon has crossed Earth's shadow
The Sun has circled the Milky Way
correct_answer: Earth has completed one orbit
explanation: A revolution is one complete trip along an orbit. Earth takes about one year to orbit the Sun.
traps: Mixing up Earth's yearly orbit with its daily rotation.

question_text: Which statement compares the inner and outer planets correctly?
choices: The inner planets are mostly rocky; the outer planets are much larger and include giant planets
All inner planets are made of gas and all outer planets are solid rock
Every planet has the same size and composition
The outer planets are closer to the Sun
correct_answer: The inner planets are mostly rocky; the outer planets are much larger and include giant planets
explanation: The four inner planets are rocky worlds. The outer planets are giant planets with deep gas or icy interiors.
traps: Assuming all planets have the same materials or that outer planets are nearer the Sun.

question_text: What are planetary rings mostly made of?
choices: Many small pieces of ice, rock, and dust orbiting a planet
A single solid hoop made of metal
Clouds floating in Earth's atmosphere
Light painted around a planet
correct_answer: Many small pieces of ice, rock, and dust orbiting a planet
explanation: A ring system is made of countless small particles orbiting a planet, not one solid ring.
traps: Imagining a planet's ring as a rigid, unbroken object.

question_text: Why can two planets at similar distances from the Sun have very different surface temperatures?
choices: Their atmospheres and surfaces can trap or reflect different amounts of heat
They must be the same temperature if their orbits are similar
Their temperatures are set by their names
Only their moons affect their temperatures
correct_answer: Their atmospheres and surfaces can trap or reflect different amounts of heat
explanation: Distance matters, but atmospheric composition, clouds, and surface properties also affect how much heat a planet keeps.
traps: Assuming distance from the Sun is the only factor controlling temperature.

question_text: Which description best fits the solar system?
choices: The Sun and the objects held in orbit by its gravity
Only the eight planets
All stars visible from Earth
A group of planets that do not orbit a star
correct_answer: The Sun and the objects held in orbit by its gravity
explanation: The solar system includes the Sun, planets, dwarf planets, moons, and many smaller bodies bound to the Sun by gravity.
traps: Leaving out moons and small bodies or including every star in the galaxy.

question_text: How did the Sun and planets begin forming?
choices: From a large cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under gravity
When Earth broke apart into the planets
When the Moon pulled stars out of the sky
From a single comet that melted
correct_answer: From a large cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under gravity
explanation: About 4.6 billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed; the Sun formed at its center and leftover material formed planets and smaller bodies.
traps: Thinking planets formed from pieces of Earth or from one comet.

question_text: What is a comet's nucleus?
choices: Its solid central body made of ice, dust, and rocky material
The bright tail that points away from the Sun
A small star inside the comet
The comet's orbit around Earth
correct_answer: Its solid central body made of ice, dust, and rocky material
explanation: The nucleus is a comet's solid core. A cloud of gas and dust can form around it when the comet warms near the Sun.
traps: Calling the tail or the surrounding cloud the nucleus.

question_text: Why did the material between Mars and Jupiter not become one large planet?
choices: Jupiter's gravity disturbed the material as it tried to gather together
The Sun blew all the rock away
Earth's Moon pulled it into Earth
The asteroids were made of air
correct_answer: Jupiter's gravity disturbed the material as it tried to gather together
explanation: Jupiter's strong gravity helped prevent the material in the main asteroid belt from accumulating into a single planet.
traps: Assuming the belt is debris from a planet that definitely exploded.

question_text: What is the coma around a comet?
choices: A fuzzy cloud of gas and dust released from its nucleus
A crater left by a collision
The path a comet follows around Earth
A hard shell made of pure metal
correct_answer: A fuzzy cloud of gas and dust released from its nucleus
explanation: As the comet warms, escaping gas and dust form a temporary cloud called a coma around its nucleus.
traps: Confusing the coma with the comet's nucleus or tail.

question_text: Why are many asteroids irregularly shaped?
choices: They are too small for their own gravity to pull them into a round shape
They are made of soft clouds
They spin only once every billion years
The Sun stretches them into triangles
correct_answer: They are too small for their own gravity to pull them into a round shape
explanation: Many asteroids are small enough that their gravity cannot overcome the strength of their rocky material and make them spherical.
traps: Assuming every object in space must be round.

question_text: What is the Kuiper Belt?
choices: A distant region beyond Neptune containing many icy bodies
A ring of rocks between Earth and Mars
The Sun's bright outer atmosphere
A group of moons around Jupiter
correct_answer: A distant region beyond Neptune containing many icy bodies
explanation: The Kuiper Belt lies beyond Neptune's orbit and contains many small icy worlds, including dwarf planets.
traps: Confusing the Kuiper Belt with the main asteroid belt.

question_text: What do we call a piece of space rock that survives its trip through the atmosphere and reaches the ground?
choices: A meteorite
A comet
A nebula
A solar flare
correct_answer: A meteorite
explanation: A meteoroid is in space; the streak of light in the atmosphere is a meteor; a surviving piece on the ground is a meteorite.
traps: Using meteor, meteoroid, and meteorite as if they mean exactly the same thing.

question_text: Which comparison between a typical asteroid and a comet is most accurate?
choices: Asteroids are mostly rocky or metallic; comets contain substantial ice as well as dust and rock
Asteroids are made of air; comets are made of stars
Asteroids orbit Earth; comets orbit the Moon
They are both planets with solid surfaces
correct_answer: Asteroids are mostly rocky or metallic; comets contain substantial ice as well as dust and rock
explanation: Asteroids are generally rocky or metallic, while comets contain ice mixed with dust and rocky material.
traps: Assuming every small solar-system body has the same composition.

question_text: What is a galaxy?
choices: A huge system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter held together by gravity
A single star with several planets
A cloud that circles Earth
A group of moons around one planet
correct_answer: A huge system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter held together by gravity
explanation: Galaxies are enormous systems containing stars and other matter bound together by gravity.
traps: Confusing a galaxy with a solar system.

question_text: Which galaxy is our solar system part of?
choices: The Milky Way
Andromeda
The Whirlpool Galaxy
The Sombrero Galaxy
correct_answer: The Milky Way
explanation: Our Sun and its planets are in the Milky Way galaxy.
traps: Mixing up our home galaxy with nearby or famous galaxies.

question_text: How does the size of the Milky Way compare with our solar system?
choices: The Milky Way is vastly larger and contains many stars and planetary systems
The solar system is larger than the Milky Way
They are about the same size
The Milky Way is only the size of Earth's orbit
correct_answer: The Milky Way is vastly larger and contains many stars and planetary systems
explanation: The solar system is one small part of the Milky Way, which spans roughly 100,000 light-years across.
traps: Confusing a galaxy with one planetary system.

question_text: What kind of galaxy is the Milky Way?
choices: A barred spiral galaxy
A perfect cube galaxy
A single ring with no stars
A tiny cluster of planets
correct_answer: A barred spiral galaxy
explanation: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with a bar-shaped region of stars through its center.
traps: Thinking a galaxy is shaped like its name or like a planetary orbit.

question_text: Does the Sun stay still within the Milky Way?
choices: No; the Sun and solar system orbit the center of the Milky Way
Yes; the Sun is at the exact center of the galaxy
No; the Sun orbits Earth
Yes; stars in a galaxy never move
correct_answer: No; the Sun and solar system orbit the center of the Milky Way
explanation: Our solar system travels around the Milky Way's center, taking hundreds of millions of years to complete one orbit.
traps: Assuming the Sun is at the center of the galaxy or that stars do not move.

question_text: Why can the Milky Way look like a pale band across a dark sky?
choices: We are looking through the crowded disk of our galaxy, where many distant stars blend together
It is a cloud of water vapor around Earth
It is sunlight reflected by the Moon
It is a line painted across space
correct_answer: We are looking through the crowded disk of our galaxy, where many distant stars blend together
explanation: From inside the Milky Way's disk, many distant stars in that direction appear as a faint, milky band, especially under dark skies.
traps: Mistaking the band for a nearby cloud or a solid structure.

question_text: Are all the stars we see in the night sky part of the Milky Way?
choices: Nearly all individual stars we see without a telescope are in the Milky Way
No; most visible stars are in other galaxies
Yes; every bright point is a planet
No; stars only exist outside galaxies
correct_answer: Nearly all individual stars we see without a telescope are in the Milky Way
explanation: The stars visible as individual points to the unaided eye are almost all relatively nearby stars in our own galaxy.
traps: Assuming ordinary visible stars are usually outside our galaxy.

question_text: Why do astronomers use light-years to describe the size of a galaxy?
choices: A light-year is a distance unit useful for the enormous distances light travels in space
A light-year measures how long a galaxy shines
A light-year is the age of a star
A light-year is how fast a planet spins
correct_answer: A light-year is a distance unit useful for the enormous distances light travels in space
explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers; it measures distance, not time.
traps: Reading 'year' in light-year and concluding it is a time measurement.

question_text: What is a star in a galaxy?
choices: A hot ball of gas that produces energy and light
A cold rock that reflects all its light
A moon orbiting a planet
A cloud of dust with no gravity
correct_answer: A hot ball of gas that produces energy and light
explanation: Stars are massive, hot balls of gas that release energy, mostly through nuclear fusion in their cores.
traps: Confusing stars with planets, which mainly reflect starlight.

question_text: What helps hold the Milky Way together?
choices: Gravity acting among its stars, gas, dust, and dark matter
A solid shell around the galaxy
The magnetic pull of Earth's poles
The pressure of air between the stars
correct_answer: Gravity acting among its stars, gas, dust, and dark matter
explanation: Gravity binds the matter in a galaxy and shapes the movement of its stars and gas.
traps: Imagining a galaxy has a solid edge or is held together by air.
